zh.summary: 從咖啡廳與主管訊息案例，分辨可信線索、身分驗證、授權與最小權限，串起社交工程、風險與證據。

sourceBody.text: Social Engineering & Human Trust
Module 09：Social Engineering（社交工程）
這堂課，我們不只要了解「駭客如何利用人際信任」，更要把前面學過的 CEH 知識串成一套完整的資安思考架構。
一、先說結論：駭客不一定要破解密碼，也可以說服你替他開門
想像一間公司有非常完善的資訊安全措施：

items: 員工帳號都有密碼保護。
重要資料只有特定人員能讀取。
所有電腦都定期更新安全修補程式。

sourceBody.text: 這間公司就安全了嗎？
不一定。因為駭客可能根本不需要攻破任何系統。
他可能只需要打電話給一名員工：
「你好，我是資訊部門的工程師。你的帳號出現異常，我需要你配合驗證，否則帳號可能會被停用。」
如果員工相信了對方，主動提供驗證碼或執行危險操作，就可能讓原本的安全措施失去作用。
這就是 Social Engineering（社交工程）的核心。
依照 NIST 的定義，社交工程是透過欺騙及建立信任，誘使他人洩漏敏感資訊、提供未經授權的存取，或參與詐欺行為。[NIST Computer Security Resource Center](https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/social_engineering)
今天最重要的三句話
① 信任（Trust）不等於身分驗證（Authentication）。
你認為對方是主管，不代表他確實是主管。
② 身分驗證（Authentication）不等於授權（Authorization）。
即使對方真的是主管，也不代表他有權要求你提供所有資料。
③ 社交工程不是獨立的攻擊領域，而是可能串起情報蒐集、身分冒用、未授權存取及資料外洩的關鍵環節。
這第三點，就是我們將 M09 與前面 CEH 課程連結的核心。
二、理解社交工程最重要的觀念：信任、驗證與授權是不同的事
這是整堂課最重要的部分。
想像咖啡廳的員工收到一則訊息：
「我是店長，現在需要你把會員名單傳給我。」
員工必須回答四個問題。

sourceBody.alt: M09-01 信任不是授權：重要行動必須經過四道關卡 看起來像本人，是「線索」；確認身分與核准這件事，才是「證據與決策」。 01 外觀與說法 Trust Cues 主管頭像、制服、聲音 知道姓名與內部事情 可能讓人覺得可信 但不能證明真實身分 02 確認身分 Authentication 使用事先已知的管道 核實現在是誰在要求 不使用訊息附的新電話 必要時查證帳號狀態 03 確認行動授權 Authorization 確認這件事是否被核准 資料能否交給這個人 核准目的地是否正確 急件也不能省略流程 04 限制執行範圍 Least Privilege 只提供必要的資料 僅使用核准的管道 記錄執行時間與內容 有疑慮就暫停並通報 危險捷徑： 看起來像主管 → 直接上傳敏感文件 這條路跳過身分驗證與授權；就算對方真的是主管，也可能違反資料處理規定。 CEH M09-01  •  概念圖 1 / 4

sourceBody.text: 第一關：Trust Cues（可信線索）
你看到對方的 LINE 頭像是店長，名字也正確。
甚至對方傳來一段語音，聲音跟店長一模一樣。
這些資訊能證明什麼？
只能證明：對方呈現了一些與店長相符的特徵。
這些特徵可能是真實的，也可能來自公開資訊、帳號遭接管，或 AI 語音合成。
第二關：Authentication（身分驗證）
現在你必須確認：
「這個要求真的是店長本人發出的嗎？」
你可以透過公司原本的通訊錄，使用事先確認過的聯絡方式向店長查證。
不過要注意，這種做法是組織流程中的身分查核，不一定具有正式資訊系統身分驗證機制的保證強度。
在資訊系統中，Authentication 通常是透過密碼、Passkey、憑證等驗證方式，確認使用者是否具備相應的身分證明。[NIST Computer Security Resource Center](https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/authentication)
第三關：Authorization（授權）
假設你已經確認：
「沒錯，真的是店長本人。」
就可以立即傳送會員名單嗎？
還不行。
你還需要確認：
「店長有沒有權限要求這次資料移轉？」
例如公司規定，會員個資只能透過經過核准的系統分享，即使店長本人要求員工使用私人雲端硬碟傳送，也可能不符合資料處理規定。
這就是 Authentication 與 Authorization 的差別。
前者問「你是誰」，後者問「你被允許做什麼」。
第四關：Least Privilege（最小權限原則）
即使要求是合法、經過授權的，也不代表必須提供全部資料。
假設店長只需要會員人數統計，你就不應直接提供包含姓名、電話、住址的完整會員資料庫。
完成工作需要多少權限，就只提供必要的權限與資料。
這個觀念可以直接呼應之前的 CEH M01-06：Security Controls 與 Defense in Depth。
三、社交工程究竟如何影響人的判斷？
我們可以將社交工程理解成一個簡化的因果流程：
建立可信感 → 影響情緒或判斷 → 誘導特定行動 → 產生安全風險。
例如：
某人自稱資訊部門主管，要求你提供帳號驗證碼。
在這段互動中，可能同時存在三種心理影響：

rows: 身分與權限是否經過核實？
五分鐘內不處理就停權
是否有正式的緊急處理流程？
我知道你的主管與工作內容
這些資訊是否可能從其他來源取得？

sourceBody.text: 此外，還有群體認同（其他人都做了）、互惠（我先幫你一個忙）、恐懼及同情等影響方式。
值得注意的是，這些並不是社交工程必定依序出現的階段，也不是單憑某個特徵就能認定對方在詐騙。
真正重要的問題是：
這些心理因素，是否正在讓我們跳過原本應有的安全檢查？
社交工程有哪些常見形式？
社交工程不只包含釣魚郵件。
例如，Pretexting（假借情境）是編造一個合理身分與理由，誘使對方配合；Baiting（誘餌攻擊）是利用好奇心或好處吸引人採取行動；Tailgating（尾隨進入）則可能利用人們替後方陌生人開門的習慣，進入受限制的實體區域。
Phishing（釣魚）是其中一個重要類別，經常透過電子郵件、網站、通訊軟體或語音，誘使使用者提供資訊或執行危險操作。
下一堂 M09-02 會深入釣魚、魚叉式釣魚與鯨釣的差別。
四、重要的 CEH 知識串聯：攻擊者可能如何從 M02 走到 M09？
接下來將前面學過的章節放在同一張地圖上。
補充說明：以下是跨章知識關聯，不代表讀者已完成這些章節；新路線先學 M09，再接 M02、M03、M04 等章節。沒有學過的部分，先掌握它在地圖上的用途即可。

sourceBody.text: 這張圖提供兩個觀察角度。
角度 A：攻擊者如何串接不同技術？
假設攻擊者想取得公司的機密資料。
第一步：M02 — Footprinting & Reconnaissance（足跡探查與情報蒐集）
他可能透過公開網站得知公司主管姓名、員工職務與近期活動。
這些資訊本身不一定是機密，但可以被用來設計更可信的冒充情境。
第二步：M09 — Social Engineering（社交工程）
攻擊者利用取得的資訊冒充主管，要求員工提供公司帳號或下載不明程式。
此時，攻擊者未必已經成功進入系統。
第三步：M06 — System Hacking（系統入侵）
假設員工真的交出登入憑證，攻擊者又成功通過相關安全檢查，就可能發生未經授權的帳號存取。
注意：取得密碼不等於一定成功登入。MFA、條件式存取及其他安全控制，都可能阻擋後續入侵。
第四步：M01-01 — CIA Triad（三大資訊安全目標）
如果攻擊者成功存取並下載機密資料，會涉及 Confidentiality（機密性）。
如果進一步竄改資料，會涉及 Integrity（完整性）。
如果使服務無法正常使用，則會涉及 Availability（可用性）。
這不是一條每次都必然發生的攻擊鏈，而是一個方便分析因果關係的例子。
角度 B：之前學過的 M03、M04、M05 在哪裡？
它們提供的是其他技術觀察角度。
M03 的網路掃描讓我們了解有哪些主機或服務開放；M04 的列舉讓我們進一步了解 DNS、SMB、帳號或服務提供的資訊；M05 的弱點分析則協助判斷系統、設定與流程中的安全缺口。
社交工程不一定需要掃描或列舉，但這些階段得到的資訊，有時也可能被用於冒充與欺騙。
呼應 M01-05：MITRE ATT&CK
還記得我們學過 MITRE ATT&CK 嗎？
它主要是用來描述攻擊者的戰術目標，以及達成目標的具體技術。
社交工程是一個廣泛的概念，而 Phishing 是其中一種攻擊技術。
例如 MITRE ATT&CK 將 Phishing 列為 T1566，其子技術包含：

rows: 用有害附件進行針對性釣魚
用惡意連結進行針對性釣魚
透過第三方服務傳送釣魚訊息
透過語音進行針對性釣魚

sourceBody.text: 這些技術被 MITRE 歸在 Initial Access（初始存取）戰術之下，但不代表每一次社交工程都一定能建立初始存取。[MITRE ATT&CK](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/)
因此，未來閱讀資安事件報告時，你可以同時問兩件事：
「這個行為在整體攻擊中扮演什麼角色？」
「它對應到哪一種具體 ATT&CK 技術？」
這就是我們在 M01-05 學習 ATT&CK 的實際用途。
五、實際情境：主管傳來一段 AI 語音，要求你上傳文件
現在進行一次完整的模擬。
假設你是某間公司的行政人員。
上午收到一則 LINE 訊息。
對方使用主管的照片，並傳來一段聲音極為相似的語音：
「我現在在開會，急著處理一件事。你先把會員資料上傳到這個網址，晚一點我再跟你解釋。」
當你表示懷疑時，對方又說：
「不然你打這支電話來確認。」
這時候應該怎麼辦？

sourceBody.alt: 情境演練 收到「主管」要求上傳內部文件，下一步怎麼做？ 可疑訊息 「現在把會員名單傳到新網址，這是緊急交辦！」 附主管照片、熟悉語音、甚至提供「驗證用」新電話號碼。 遇到高風險要求，你選擇哪一條處理路線？ 錯誤路線 正確路線 ✕  容易犯的錯誤 直接打訊息附上的新電話 可能仍由冒充者接聽 換成電話或另一個 App， 不代表脫離了對方的控制。 ✓  更安全的處理方式 ① 找事先保存的主管聯絡方式 ② 確認「這次」是否真的要傳資料 ③ 核准範圍、目的地、程序再確認 ④ 有疑慮時先暫停並通報 判斷原則：換通訊工具 ≠ 獨立驗證；來源獨立、內容具體、權限正當才是重點。
sourceBody.caption: 獨立驗證的決策流程｜使用者原始 SVG，圖中文字維持原樣。

sourceBody.text: 關鍵觀念：Independent Verification（獨立驗證）
所謂獨立驗證，重點不是換一種通訊工具，而是驗證資訊必須來自不依賴可疑訊息的可信來源。
例如：
對方提供一個新電話號碼，你照著撥打，即使有人接聽並聲稱自己是主管，也不構成可靠的獨立確認。
更合理的處理方式，是使用公司原有的通訊錄、已知的主管聯絡方式，或正式的內部核准系統，查證這一次具體要求。

美國 FBI 也曾針對冒充政府高階人員的惡意訊息提出警告，建議收件者自行尋找可靠的聯絡方式確認身分，而不是只依賴訊息提供的資料。[FBI](https://www.fbi.gov/investigate/cyber/alerts/2025/senior-us-officials-continue-to-be-impersonated-in-malicious-messaging-campaign)
然而，還有更深一層的問題。
即使主管本人確認了要求，你依然需要確認資料處理是否符合組織規定。
這代表我們至少應區分：
確認要求來源 → 確認行動授權 → 確認資料範圍與目的地。
而對於特別敏感的操作，組織可以再加入雙人覆核等控制，避免單一帳號或通訊管道遭冒用時，整個核准機制跟著失效。
AI Deepfake 改變了什麼？
AI 語音合成、圖片生成與深偽影像，可以提高冒充內容的可信程度。
但我們不應把安全防護建立在「我應該聽得出來是不是 AI」這個假設上。
因為即使是真的主管親口提出要求，也可能存在超出權限、違反流程或誤傳資料的風險。
要驗證的是行動本身是否可信、正當且經過核准，而不只是媒體內容是否由 AI 生成。
六、呼應 M01-02：如何用資產、威脅、弱點與風險分析這起事件？
現在換成資安工程師的角色。
假設我們必須向主管說明這起事件的風險，而不只是告訴大家要小心。
可以使用之前 M01-02 的四個概念。

headers: 這起社交工程事件的對應內容
rows: 會員個資、員工帳號與公司資訊系統
冒充主管，誘使員工將資料送往未經核准的位置
對敏感資料移轉缺乏必要的查證與核准流程
資料可能被未授權取得，以及因此造成的損害

sourceBody.text: 注意這裡的重要區別：
如果公司確實沒有查證流程，這是一項可能被利用的流程弱點。
但僅僅收到一則可疑訊息，不足以證明公司存在該弱點，更不足以證明已經造成資料外洩。
我們需要區分：
「可能發生什麼？」
「實際觀察到什麼？」
「哪些結果已經得到證據支持？」
這也是未來進行資安稽核、滲透測試及事件調查時非常重要的專業判斷。
七、呼應 M01-06 與 M01-07：如何真正防止社交工程？
我們之前學過 Defense in Depth（縱深防禦）。
它的意思不是安裝越多資安軟體越好，而是在不同位置安排互補的防護措施。

sourceBody.alt: M01 × M09 縱深防禦：不是多買工具，而是安排互補關卡 每一層即使失效，下一層仍有機會阻擋、發現、降低或修復損害。 階段 對應控制與白話理解 連回 CEH 01 事前 文件傳送必須有核准流程 不依賴員工自行猜測主管意圖 M01-06  預防控制 02 當下 用可信管道核實本次要求 主管照片、聲音不等於身分證據 M09-01  獨立驗證 03 執行 最小權限＋核准目的地 就算判斷失誤也盡可能限制影響 M01-06  限制損害 04 發現異常 容易求助的通報管道 通報不責備，能讓問題早點曝光 M01-07  偵測／通報 05 事後 保存紀錄、應變、復原 分清楚「點擊」與「真的遭入侵」 M01-07  調查／復原 證據界線 收到可疑訊息 ≠ 已遭入侵；點擊連結 ≠ 一定中毒；未上傳 ≠ 全系統安全。 CEH M09-01  •  概念圖 4 / 4

sourceBody.text: 第一層：預防（Prevention）
組織事先訂定敏感資料存取與移轉的核准程序。
例如，禁止透過個人通訊軟體直接傳送完整會員資料。
第二層：驗證（Verification）
員工收到異常要求時，透過可信管道查證。
高風險操作可能需要額外的核准。
第三層：限制（Limitation）
即使有員工受騙，也透過最小權限、存取控制與適當的資料外洩防護措施，減少可能造成的損害。
第四層：偵測與通報（Detection & Reporting）
讓員工知道發現異常時應該聯絡誰。
如果有人誤點連結，不應因為擔心被責備，就選擇隱瞞事件。
及早通報才能讓資安人員判斷是否需要停止工作階段、撤銷憑證，或執行其他應變措施。
第五層：調查與復原（Investigation & Recovery）
這就回到 M01-07 的 Incident Response（事件應變）。
假設員工已經把文件傳出，公司需要調查：
哪些資料被傳送？何時發生？目的地是什麼？是否還有其他帳號或系統受到影響？
調查必須以紀錄與證據為依據。
例如：
「點擊過連結」不等於「一定感染惡意程式」。
「帳號曾經登入」也不代表「登入者一定是帳號持有人本人」。
「已撤銷外部分享權限」更不能直接證明對方從未下載或保留資料。
這些差別決定了資安事件調查的可信度。
八、今天的 CEH 知識整合
回顧這堂課，可以建立以下完整的概念鏈：
M02 情報蒐集 → M09 利用信任 → 可能造成 M06 未授權存取 → 影響 M01 的 CIA 安全目標。
另一方面，防守者透過：
M01-02 風險分析 → M01-06 安全控制 → M09 獨立驗證 → M01-07 事件應變。
來降低攻擊成功的可能性與影響。
這是今天應該建立在腦中的兩條主要路線。
特別注意，社交工程與技術性入侵可以互相配合，但並不是每次社交工程都需要技術性弱點，也不是每次攻擊都會經過所有章節。
對資安工程師而言，最重要的不是看到一封可疑郵件就直接認定發生入侵，而是能分析行為、權限、風險與證據之間的關係。
九、學習檢核：你能把前面學過的 CEH 知識一起用上嗎？
情境：
某公司會計收到一則使用財務主管照片的 LINE 訊息。
對方附上一段極為相似的主管語音，要求立即將一份內部財務報表傳到新的雲端網址。
當會計表示懷疑時，對方回覆：
「你不相信就打我剛剛給你的新電話，我親自跟你確認。」
請試著回答：
問題 1｜Authentication
為什麼使用訊息提供的新電話回撥，不能視為可靠的獨立驗證？你會怎麼做？
問題 2｜Authorization
假設你透過公司原本的聯絡方式，確認要求確實來自財務主管。這樣是否就能直接傳送報表？還需要確認什麼？
問題 3｜CEH M01-02
請指出這起事件的一項 Asset、一項 Threat，以及一項可能存在的 Vulnerability。
問題 4｜CEH M01-01
假設會計真的將機密報表傳給未經授權的第三人，主要涉及 CIA Triad 的哪一項安全目標？為什麼？
問題 5｜M01-07 Incident Response
假設會計只點擊了新網址，但沒有輸入帳號、下載檔案或上傳報表。你認為目前有哪些事實已經確認？還需要哪些證據，才能判斷是否發生安全事件？
請先用自己的話回答，我會依序評估你的理解，並指出哪些觀念已經掌握、哪些需要補強。
補充：以下提供參考解答，預設收合。看過答案不代表已作答或已理解；請先用自己的話判斷，再展開對照。

sourceBody.summary: 問題 1 參考解答｜身分驗證
paragraphs: 不能，因為新電話也是可疑訊息提供的，仍可能由同一個冒充者控制。應使用公司原有通訊錄或事先確認的聯絡方式，核實「這一次要求」，必要時走正式核准流程；不是只換成電話就算獨立驗證。

sourceBody.summary: 問題 2 參考解答｜授權
paragraphs: 不能直接傳送。還要確認主管是否有權要求這次移轉、報表能否提供給該對象、目的地是否核准，以及是否只提供工作必要的資料。真的主管也不能跳過公司規定；高風險操作可依制度加上雙人覆核。

sourceBody.summary: 問題 3 參考解答｜資產、威脅與弱點
paragraphs: Asset 可以是內部財務報表；Threat 是有人冒充主管，誘使會計把報表傳到未核准的位置；可能的 Vulnerability 是敏感資料移轉缺乏查證或核准流程。最後一項仍是待查假設，不能只憑收到訊息就認定公司一定有此弱點。

sourceBody.summary: 問題 4 參考解答｜CIA 安全目標
paragraphs: 主要是 Confidentiality（機密性），因為不該取得報表的人拿到了機密資料。題目沒有說資料遭竄改或服務中斷，因此不能直接把完整性、可用性受損也當成已確認事實。

sourceBody.summary: 問題 5 參考解答｜事件應變與證據
paragraphs: 依情境陳述，目前知道會計點過網址，並表示沒有輸入帳號、下載檔案或上傳報表；這些行為仍可用紀錄核對。點擊不等於已中毒，沒有手動下載也不能證明完全安全。應依組織流程通報、保留訊息與時間，查瀏覽器導向與下載紀錄、端點偵測、網路連線和帳號登入／工作階段紀錄，確認是否有自動下載、異常程式或未授權存取。證據不足時保留待查，不用真實帳號重開可疑網站來測試。

en.summary: Use café and manager-message scenarios to distinguish trust cues, authentication, authorization and least privilege, connecting social engineering with risk and evidence.

sourceBody.text: Social Engineering & Human Trust
Module 09: Social Engineering

In this lesson, we will not only understand how attackers exploit interpersonal trust, but also connect the CEH knowledge introduced earlier into a complete framework for thinking about information security.
1. The main point: attackers do not always need to crack a password—they may persuade you to open the door
Imagine a company with very thorough information-security measures:

items: Only designated staff can read important information.
All computers receive security patches regularly.

sourceBody.text: Is the company secure now?
Not necessarily. An attacker might not need to break into any system at all.
They may only need to call an employee:
“Hello, I am an engineer from IT. We have detected a problem with your account. I need you to help verify it, or your account may be suspended.”
If the employee trusts the caller and voluntarily provides a verification code or performs a dangerous action, the existing safeguards may be undermined.
That is the core of social engineering.

Under NIST's definition, social engineering uses deception and trust-building to induce someone to disclose sensitive information, provide unauthorized access, or participate in fraud. [NIST Computer Security Resource Center](https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/social_engineering)
Today's three most important statements
① Trust is not the same as authentication.
Believing that someone is your manager does not mean they actually are your manager.
② Authentication is not the same as authorization.
Even if the person really is your manager, that does not mean they have authority to ask you for every piece of information.
③ Social engineering is not an isolated attack domain. It can be a key link connecting intelligence gathering, impersonation, unauthorized access and data disclosure.
This third point is central to connecting M09 with the earlier CEH lessons.
2. The most important distinction in social engineering: trust, verification and authorization are different things
This is the most important part of the lesson.
Imagine that a café employee receives a message:
“I am the store manager. I need you to send me the membership list now.”
The employee needs to answer four questions.

sourceBody.alt: M09-01. Trust is not authorization: important actions must pass four gates. Looking like someone is a clue; confirming identity and approving the action are evidence and decisions. Gate 1, appearance and claims: a manager’s photo, uniform, voice, name or internal knowledge may appear credible but cannot prove identity. Gate 2, authentication: use a previously known channel, verify who is making this request, do not use a new number supplied in the message, and check account status if necessary. Gate 3, authorization: check approval for this action, whether this person may receive the data and whether the destination is approved. Urgency does not remove process requirements. Gate 4, least privilege: provide only necessary information through approved channels, record the time and content, and pause and report doubts. Dangerous shortcut: looks like the manager → directly upload sensitive documents. This skips authentication and authorization; even a real manager’s request can violate data-handling rules. Concept diagram 1 of 4.
sourceBody.caption: Trust cues, authentication, authorization and least privilege | Original user-supplied Chinese SVG; image text is preserved unchanged.
sourceBody.openLabel: Open the original image to enlarge

sourceBody.text: Gate 1: Trust cues
You see the store manager's photo as the sender's LINE profile picture, and the name is correct too.
The sender even provides a voice message that sounds exactly like the store manager.
What does this information prove?
Only this: the sender has presented some characteristics that match the store manager.
These characteristics could be genuine, but they could also come from public information, an account takeover, or AI voice synthesis.
Gate 2: Authentication
Now you need to establish:
“Did the store manager really make this request?”
You can check with the manager using the company's existing directory and previously verified contact details.
However, note that this is identity checking within an organizational process. It does not necessarily provide the same assurance level as a formal information-system authentication mechanism.

In information systems, authentication typically uses passwords, passkeys, certificates or other methods to check whether a user possesses the corresponding proof of identity. [NIST Computer Security Resource Center](https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/authentication)
Gate 3: Authorization
Suppose you have established:
“Yes, this really is the store manager.”
Can you send the membership list immediately?
Not yet.
You still need to check:
“Does the manager have authority to request this particular data transfer?”

For example, company policy may permit sharing members' personal data only through approved systems. Even a genuine request from the manager to send it through a personal cloud drive could violate data-handling rules.
That is the difference between authentication and authorization.
The former asks “Who are you?” The latter asks “What are you allowed to do?”
Gate 4: Least privilege
Even a legitimate, authorized request does not mean you must provide all the data.
If the manager only needs a count of members, you should not simply supply the complete membership database containing names, phone numbers and addresses.
Provide only the permissions and information necessary to complete the work.
This directly connects to CEH M01-06: Security Controls and Defense in Depth.
3. How does social engineering influence people's judgment?
We can understand social engineering through a simplified cause-and-effect sequence:
Build a sense of credibility → influence emotions or judgment → induce a specific action → create a security risk.
For example:
Someone claims to be the head of IT and asks you to provide an account verification code.
Three psychological influences may be present at the same time in this interaction:

rows: I am the head of IT.
Have identity and permissions been verified?
Your account will be suspended unless you act within five minutes.
Is there a formal emergency-handling process?
I know your manager and what you do at work.
Could this information have come from other sources?

sourceBody.text: Other influences include social proof (“Everyone else has done it”), reciprocity (“I helped you first”), fear and sympathy.
Importantly, these are not stages that must appear in a fixed order in every social-engineering attempt. Nor does any single feature prove that someone is committing fraud.
The question that really matters is:
Are these psychological factors causing us to skip security checks that should normally apply?
What are common forms of social engineering?
Social engineering includes more than phishing emails.

For example, pretexting invents a plausible identity and reason to get someone to cooperate. Baiting uses curiosity or an apparent benefit to entice someone into acting. Tailgating may exploit people's habit of holding a door for a stranger behind them to enter a restricted physical area.
Phishing is one important category. It often uses email, websites, messaging services or voice to induce users to disclose information or perform dangerous actions.
The next lesson, M09-02, explores the differences between phishing, spear phishing and whaling in depth.
4. Connecting CEH knowledge: how might an attacker move from M02 to M09?
Next, we will place the chapters introduced earlier on a single map.

Supplement: these are cross-chapter knowledge connections, not a claim that the reader has completed these chapters. The new route studies M09 before M02, M03, M04 and the subsequent chapters. For unfamiliar material, first understand what it contributes to this map.

sourceBody.alt: CEH knowledge map. The orange-red path is one possible attack route, not a mandatory sequence for every incident. M02 Footprinting: collect public information such as managers’ names, employee roles, social posts and activities. M09 Social Engineering: exploit trust through impersonation and plausible urgency. M06 System Hacking: unauthorized behavior may follow if the attack succeeds, through account acquisition or induced execution. M01 CIA Triad: assess confidentiality loss, integrity damage or availability impact. Other technical perspectives do not imply every attempt includes scanning or enumeration: M01-04 Attack Surface asks which contact points could be exploited; M03 Scanning asks which services are exposed; M04 Enumeration examines DNS, SMB and account clues; M05 Vulnerability Analysis identifies technical and process gaps. Defense also combines M01-03 Authorization and ROE, including permission before testing; M01-06 Defense in Depth, including verification, least privilege and two-person review; and M01-07 Incident Response, including evidence preservation, harm limitation and recovery. M09 targets human judgment and processes; M02/M04 may supply persuasive material, while M01 controls block attacks and limit harm. Concept diagram 2 of 4.
sourceBody.caption: Social engineering within the CEH attack-and-defense framework | Original user-supplied Chinese SVG; image text is preserved unchanged.
sourceBody.openLabel: Open the original image to enlarge

sourceBody.text: This diagram offers two perspectives.
Perspective A: how do attackers connect different techniques?
Suppose an attacker wants to obtain a company's confidential information.
Step 1: M02 — Footprinting & Reconnaissance
They may learn managers' names, employees' roles and recent company activities from public websites.
This information is not necessarily confidential by itself, but it can be used to design a more convincing impersonation scenario.
Step 2: M09 — Social Engineering
The attacker uses the information to impersonate a manager and asks an employee to supply company account information or download an unknown program.
At this point, the attacker has not necessarily gained access to the system.
Step 3: M06 — System Hacking
If the employee actually hands over login credentials and the attacker successfully passes the relevant security checks, unauthorized account access may occur.
Remember: obtaining a password does not guarantee a successful login. Multi-factor authentication (MFA), conditional access and other security controls may still block the subsequent intrusion.
Step 4: M01-01 — CIA Triad, the three information-security objectives
If the attacker successfully accesses and downloads confidential information, confidentiality is affected.
If they also alter the information, integrity is affected.
If they make a service unavailable for normal use, availability is affected.
This is not an attack chain that inevitably occurs every time. It is an example that helps us analyze cause and effect.
Perspective B: where do M03, M04 and M05 fit?
They provide other technical perspectives.

Network scanning in M03 helps us understand which hosts or services are exposed. Enumeration in M04 reveals more about information provided by DNS, SMB, accounts or services. Vulnerability analysis in M05 helps us assess security gaps in systems, configurations and processes.
Social engineering does not necessarily require scanning or enumeration. However, information obtained through those activities may sometimes support impersonation and deception.
Connecting to M01-05: MITRE ATT&CK
Remember the introduction to MITRE ATT&CK?
Its main purpose is to describe attackers' tactical objectives and the specific techniques used to achieve them.
Social engineering is a broad concept; phishing is one attack technique within it.
For example, MITRE ATT&CK identifies Phishing as T1566, with these sub-techniques:

rows: Targeted phishing using a harmful attachment
Targeted phishing using a malicious link
Sending phishing messages through third-party services

sourceBody.text: MITRE places these techniques under the Initial Access tactic. That does not mean every social-engineering attempt successfully establishes initial access. [MITRE ATT&CK](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/)
When you read security-incident reports in the future, you can therefore ask two questions at the same time:
“What role does this behavior play in the overall attack?”
“Which specific ATT&CK technique does it correspond to?”
This is a practical use of the ATT&CK material in M01-05.
5. A practical scenario: your manager sends an AI voice message asking you to upload documents
Now let us work through a complete simulation.
Suppose you are an administrative employee at a company.
You receive a LINE message in the morning.
The sender uses your manager's photo and sends a voice message that sounds extremely similar to your manager:
“I am in a meeting and need to handle something urgently. Upload the membership data to this website first. I will explain later.”
When you express doubts, the sender adds:
“Then call this number to confirm.”
What should you do now?

sourceBody.alt: Scenario: a “manager” requests an internal-document upload. Suspicious message: “Send the membership list to this new URL now; this is urgent!” It includes a manager’s photo, familiar voice and even a new number for “verification.” Which route should you take for a high-risk request? Wrong route: directly call the new number in the message. The impersonator may still answer; changing to a phone or another app does not escape their control. Safer route: 1. Find the manager’s previously saved contact details. 2. Confirm whether this specific data transfer is really requested. 3. Recheck approved scope, destination and procedure. 4. Pause and report when in doubt. Changing communication tools is not independent verification. Independent sources, specific request content and legitimate authority are what matter.
sourceBody.caption: The independent-verification decision flow | Original user-supplied Chinese SVG; image text is preserved unchanged.
sourceBody.openLabel: Open the original image to enlarge

sourceBody.text: Key concept: independent verification
Independent verification is not about switching communication tools. The verification information must come from a trusted source that does not depend on the suspicious message.
For example:
If the sender gives you a new phone number and you call it, someone answering and claiming to be your manager still does not constitute reliable independent confirmation.
A more reasonable approach is to verify this specific request using the company's existing directory, your manager's known contact details, or the formal internal approval system.

The U.S. FBI has also warned about malicious messages impersonating senior government officials. It advises recipients to independently find reliable contact details to verify identity, rather than relying only on information supplied in the message. [FBI](https://www.fbi.gov/investigate/cyber/alerts/2025/senior-us-officials-continue-to-be-impersonated-in-malicious-messaging-campaign)
There is still another layer to consider.
Even if the manager personally confirms the request, you must still check whether the data handling follows organizational rules.
This means distinguishing at least the following:
Verify the source of the request → verify authorization for the action → verify the data scope and destination.

For particularly sensitive operations, an organization can add controls such as two-person review. This helps prevent the entire approval mechanism from failing when a single account or communication channel is impersonated or compromised.
What do AI deepfakes change?
AI voice synthesis, generated images and deepfake video can make impersonation more convincing.
But we should not base our security on the assumption that “I should be able to hear whether it is AI.”
Even a request spoken by the real manager may exceed their authority, violate procedures or risk sending data to the wrong place.
Verify whether the action itself is trustworthy, legitimate and approved—not merely whether the media was generated by AI.
6. Connecting to M01-02: how can assets, threats, vulnerabilities and risk help analyze this event?
Now take the role of a security engineer.
Suppose we need to explain the risk of this event to management, rather than simply tell everyone to be careful.
We can use the four concepts from M01-02.

headers: How it applies to this social-engineering event
rows: Members’ personal information, employee accounts and company information systems
Impersonating a manager to induce an employee to send information to an unapproved location
Lack of necessary verification and approval processes for sensitive-data transfers
The possibility of unauthorized acquisition of information and the resulting harm

sourceBody.text: Notice this important distinction:
If the company really lacks a verification process, that is a process vulnerability that might be exploited.
But receiving a suspicious message alone does not prove that the company has this vulnerability, much less that data has already been disclosed.
We need to distinguish:
“What might happen?”
“What was actually observed?”
“Which outcomes are supported by evidence?”
These distinctions are also essential professional judgments in security audits, penetration tests and incident investigations.
7. Connecting to M01-06 and M01-07: how can we actually defend against social engineering?
We previously introduced defense in depth.
This does not mean installing as much security software as possible. It means placing complementary safeguards at different points.

sourceBody.alt: M01 × M09. Defense in depth means complementary gates, not buying more tools. If one layer fails, another may still block, detect, reduce or repair harm. Beforehand: require an approval process for document transfers rather than making employees guess a manager’s intent; M01-06 preventive controls. At the time: verify this request through a trusted channel; a manager’s photo or voice is not proof of identity; M09-01 independent verification. During execution: least privilege and approved destinations limit impact even after a mistaken judgment; M01-06 harm limitation. When anomalies are noticed: provide an accessible, non-blaming reporting channel so problems surface early; M01-07 detection and reporting. Afterward: preserve records, respond and recover; distinguish clicking from actual compromise; M01-07 investigation and recovery. Evidence boundaries: a suspicious message is not proof of compromise; a click is not proof of infection; no upload is not proof that the entire system is safe. Concept diagram 4 of 4.
sourceBody.caption: Defense in depth against social engineering | Original user-supplied Chinese SVG; image text is preserved unchanged.
sourceBody.openLabel: Open the original image to enlarge

sourceBody.text: Layer 1: Prevention
The organization establishes approval procedures for accessing and transferring sensitive information in advance.
For example, it prohibits sending complete membership records directly through personal messaging services.
Layer 2: Verification
When employees receive unusual requests, they verify them through trusted channels.
High-risk operations may need additional approval.
Layer 3: Limitation
Even if an employee is deceived, least privilege, access controls and appropriate data-loss prevention measures can reduce the resulting harm.
Layer 4: Detection & Reporting
Make sure employees know whom to contact when they notice something unusual.
Someone who accidentally clicks a link should not hide the event for fear of being blamed.
Early reporting enables security staff to decide whether they need to terminate sessions, revoke credentials or take other response measures.
Layer 5: Investigation & Recovery
This returns us to incident response in M01-07.
Suppose an employee has already sent the documents. The company needs to investigate:
What information was sent? When did it happen? What was the destination? Were any other accounts or systems affected?
The investigation must be based on records and evidence.
For example:
“A link was clicked” does not mean “malware infection definitely occurred.”
“The account was used to log in” does not mean “the person logging in was definitely the account owner.”
“External sharing permission has been revoked” certainly does not by itself prove that the recipient never downloaded or retained the information.
These distinctions determine the credibility of a security-incident investigation.
8. Bringing today's CEH knowledge together
Looking back at this lesson, we can form this complete chain of concepts:
M02 intelligence gathering → M09 exploitation of trust → possible M06 unauthorized access → impact on M01's CIA security objectives.
On the defensive side, we use:
M01-02 risk analysis → M01-06 security controls → M09 independent verification → M01-07 incident response.
These reduce the likelihood and impact of a successful attack.
These are the two main paths to keep in mind from today's lesson.

Importantly, social engineering and technical intrusion can work together, but not every social-engineering attempt requires a technical vulnerability, and not every attack passes through every chapter.

For a security engineer, the essential skill is not immediately declaring an intrusion after seeing a suspicious email. It is analyzing the relationships among actions, permissions, risk and evidence.
9. Learning check: can you apply the CEH concepts together?
Scenario:
An accountant receives a LINE message using the finance manager's photo.
The sender includes a voice message sounding extremely similar to the manager and demands the immediate transfer of an internal financial report to a new cloud URL.
When the accountant expresses doubt, the sender replies:
“If you do not believe me, call the new number I just gave you. I will personally confirm it.”
Try answering the following:
Question 1 | Authentication
Why is calling back the new phone number provided in the message not reliable independent verification? What would you do?
Question 2 | Authorization
Suppose you use the company's existing contact details and confirm that the finance manager really made the request. Can you now send the report directly? What else must you check?
Question 3 | CEH M01-02
Identify one asset, one threat and one possible vulnerability in this event.
Question 4 | CEH M01-01
If the accountant really sends the confidential report to an unauthorized third party, which CIA Triad security objective is primarily affected? Why?
Question 5 | M01-07 Incident Response

Suppose the accountant only clicked the new URL, without entering account information, downloading files or uploading the report. Which facts do you think are currently established? What additional evidence is needed to judge whether a security incident occurred?
First answer in your own words. I will assess your understanding in turn and identify which concepts you have grasped and which need reinforcement.

Supplement: reference answers are provided below, collapsed by default. Reading an answer does not mean you have answered or understood it. Make your own judgment first, then expand the answer to compare.

paragraphs: No. The new number also came from the suspicious message and may still be controlled by the same impersonator. Use the company’s existing directory or previously verified contact details to check this specific request, using the formal approval process when necessary. Merely switching to a phone does not make verification independent.

Do not send it directly. Check whether the manager has authority to request this transfer, whether the recipient may receive the report, whether the destination is approved and whether you are providing only the information necessary for the work. A genuine manager cannot bypass company rules. High-risk actions can require two-person review under organizational policy.

sourceBody.summary: Question 3 reference answer | Assets, threats and vulnerabilities
paragraphs: An asset is the internal financial report. A threat is someone impersonating the manager to induce the accountant to send it to an unapproved location. A possible vulnerability is a lack of verification or approval procedures for sensitive-data transfers. The last item remains a hypothesis to investigate; receiving the message alone does not prove the company has this weakness.

sourceBody.summary: Question 4 reference answer | CIA security objectives
paragraphs: Primarily confidentiality, because someone who should not receive the report obtains confidential information. The question does not say that information was altered or a service interrupted, so integrity and availability damage must not also be treated as established facts.

sourceBody.summary: Question 5 reference answer | Incident response and evidence
paragraphs: According to the scenario, the accountant clicked the URL and reports not entering account information, downloading files or uploading the report. These actions can still be checked against records. A click does not prove infection, and no manual download does not prove complete safety. Follow organizational reporting procedures, preserve the message and timing, and examine browser redirects and download history, endpoint detections, network connections, and account login/session records for automatic downloads, unusual programs or unauthorized access. If evidence is insufficient, leave the matter under investigation. Do not reopen the suspicious site using a real account to test it.
